analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act's excise tax on medical device manufacturers and importers.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act's medical device excise tax drew 40 Republican cosponsors but died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the excise tax on medical device manufacturers and importers that Congress created as part of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, one of the taxes used to help pay for the law [S2]. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 111th Congress ended [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Medical device manufacturers and importers would gain the most: the bill would erase the excise tax on their products that Congress had created as part of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act [S2]. Removing the tax would let device companies keep more of their sales revenue [S2].

how_it_helps.text: It would eliminate the excise tax on medical device manufacturers and importers that was established by the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, allowing device companies to keep the revenue the tax would have taken
The repeal would be permanent, striking the tax provision (Section 4191 of the Internal Revenue Code) from law entirely rather than delaying it
Supporters argued the tax would raise costs in an innovative industry; the bill's own title frames the tax as a threat to medical innovation

analysis.who_pays: If the bill had passed, the federal government would have lost the revenue from the medical device excise tax, which was one of the taxes created to help pay for the Affordable Care Act's coverage expansion [S2]. That money would have had to be made up from other taxes, other ACA financing provisions, or added to deficits [S2].

drawbacks.text: Repealing the tax would remove one of the revenue sources Congress created to pay for the Affordable Care Act, meaning the lost money would have to come from other taxes, other cuts, or larger deficits

The device industry stood to benefit twice over from the Affordable Care Act, since the law's coverage expansion gave it millions of newly insured customers while this bill would have lifted its tax burden onto other payers

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated: device manufacturers would keep the revenue an excise tax would have taken from their sales [S2]. The cost is diffuse: the tax was part of how the Affordable Care Act paid for itself, so repeal would shift that burden to taxpayers and other parts of the law [S2]. The bill offered nothing in exchange for the lost revenue and no replacement funding source, which is the main honest objection to it.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: The bill would have repealed the excise tax on medical device manufacturers and importers that was created as part of the Affordable Care Act
It was introduced on April 21, 2010 and referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee, the committee that handles tax legislation
The committee took no further action; the bill's only recorded steps were its introduction and referral
The bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without ever reaching the House floor

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Affordable Care Act's financing was left intact, since the device excise tax it relied on stayed on the books [S2]. Medical device makers did not get the repeal they sought during this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Affordable Care Act's financing stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Erik Paulsen
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to repeal the medical device excise tax

for.name: 40 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (40 of 178 House Republicans)

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no markup, hearing, or floor vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and cosponsored entirely by Republicans, with no Democrats among its 40 cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would remove a tax on the industry's sales that was created to help finance the Affordable Care Act [S2]. Device makers were also among the intended beneficiaries of the law's coverage expansion, so a full repeal would let the industry keep the law's new customers while shedding its share of the cost.
